What

What Cedar Tree Health & Maintenance Involves

Cedar tree health and maintenance is the specialized care of eastern red cedar (Juniperus virginiana) and white cedar / arborvitae (Thuja occidentalis) — the conical evergreens found across NE Ohio landscapes. It covers maintenance-shape pruning to the tree's natural form, cedar-apple rust assessment, and structural hazard evaluation. Every job Aaron walks starts with a free written estimate before any cut is made.

The distinction that matters: cedars do not reliably back-bud from bare wood. Cuts have to stay in green-needled growth or just behind the green-to-bare boundary, or the tree develops permanent dead zones that never recover. That means cedar work is about shaping and preservation, not the heavy reduction you can get away with on hardwoods. When a cedar has genuinely outgrown its space, removal-and-replant is usually the better outcome than radical pruning.

Why

Four Reasons NE Ohio Homeowners Call Roubic for Cedars

The top cedar scenarios Aaron assesses each season across NE Ohio residential properties.

Cedar-Apple Rust on the Property

A fungal disease that alternates between cedars and apple/crabapple trees. Galls form on cedars, telia release in spring. If you have both species, you have a cycle to manage.

Overgrown or Badly Sheared Cedar

A cedar cut into bare wood won't re-green. Maintenance shaping keeps the conical form; heavy reduction leaves permanent dead zones.

Heart Rot at the Base

Older landscape cedars develop base heart rot over 30–50 years. Root-plate failure is the typical failure mode — visible cavities need assessment.

Thuja Hedge / Privacy Screen

White cedar (arborvitae) hedges and screens need routine maintenance shaping to stay dense, even, and healthy along a property line.

Common Cedar Questions

Cedar Tree Health & Maintenance FAQ

Five things NE Ohio homeowners want to know before booking cedar work.

Can I prune a cedar back hard?
No — cedars don't reliably back-bud from naked wood. Cuts must stay in green-needled growth. Heavy reduction creates permanent dead zones that never recover. If a cedar has outgrown its space, removal-and-replant is typically a better outcome than radical pruning.
When should cedars be pruned?
Late winter or early spring before new growth begins is ideal. Light shaping can also be performed in midsummer. Avoid pruning in late fall — fresh cuts are more vulnerable to cold damage heading into a NE Ohio winter.
What is cedar-apple rust and how does it affect my landscape?
Cedar-apple rust is a fungal disease that alternates between cedar and apple/crabapple trees. It causes galls on cedars and leaf spots and fruit damage on apples. If you have both species, you have a cedar-apple rust cycle to manage — options include cedar removal, a fungicide program on the apples, or accepting the cosmetic impact.
Do you apply fungicide for cedar-apple rust?
Roubic provides on-site assessment and a management plan, but does not currently apply fungicide ourselves. When treatment is the chosen path, we coordinate with a licensed applicator so the program is handled correctly. Where cedar removal is the better answer, we can scope that instead.
How much does cedar maintenance cost?
Cedar maintenance pruning typically runs quoted on-site depending on size and scope. White cedar (Thuja) hedge-form maintenance is priced per linear foot. Rust assessment and hazard removals are quoted on-site after Aaron walks the property.
